newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW - Mexico PAN's economic plan still vague.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Mexico PAN's economic plan still vague.

text.p: Mexico's National Action Party (PAN), which stands a chance of breaking the ruling party's 68-year grip on Congress in July's elections, has only a vague idea of what its economic platform should be, one of its top advisors said in a Reuters interview.
"The PAN doesn't have economists, it has never needed them," said Isaac Katz, professor of economics at the respected Mexico Autonomous Technological Institute (ITAM).
"It has a vision that is not wrong in general, but it is in details, added Katz, who is helping the party draw up its economic platform.

The PAN has been criticizsed by some economists for the wooliness of its economic policy. In a wide-ranging document setting out its 1997-2000 policy aims, the party only briefly mentioned economic goals, offering few specifics.

One passage read: "We suggest substituting the paternalist, omnipresent and omnipotent government with a solidarity and subsidiary government which is accountable, which encourages individual responsibility and which respects freedom."
Katz recently took on the role of economic adviser to the PAN, providing input in the drafting of an economic platform, a party spokesman said.
Katz said the PAN had adopted him as "its economist", seeking to impose a standard economic vision on a party that is widely considered pro-business but has rarely been tested.

If he has his way, it will be the sort of pure monetarism hauled straight from the University of Chicago where he studied -- free markets, flexible labor laws, stronger private property guarantees and a lean role for the government.
Katz said he advocates granting more autonomy to the central bank, taking the finance ministry out of foreign exchange management and the principle of balanced budgets.

He is not a member of the PAN, nor does he appear to hold it with much reverence. His new pupils in the party, he dubs "home economists", and when mentioning their sympathies for "capitalism with a human face", he roars with laughter during an interview conducted this week.
"Pure capitalism does have a human face," he says.
He tackles the PAN on what he sees as a deep contradiction: a liberal economic philosophy, but one that also sees the government as a safety net for the less privileged.
"No one has explained to them...it's impossible to set up (a state safety net) because of the huge income disparity that exists in Mexico," he says.

But Katz is serious about his mission, which he describes as helping the PAN draw up an economic platform that would not contradict the free market policies of President Ernesto Zedillo, but would instead deepen and strengthen them.
So far, he says, what the PAN has is a "wish list", a set of good intentions that he calls "a letter to Santa Claus".

On the other hand, he condemns Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), that has held a majority in Congress since 1929, as a defender of the status quo, beholden to entrenched labor and bureaucratic interests.
He says the PAN should push for bankruptcy laws that are more friendly to banks, and labor laws that would tackle old pro-PRI unions and give firms more freedom to hire and fire.
Competition should be introduced into public health and education, with private firms paid by the government to administer schools and hospitals.
The central bank, Banco de Mexico, should be made more autonomous and the Finance Ministry stripped of any role in setting foreign exchange policy, he said.
He agreed with the bank's current policy of gradually lowering inflation and said the existing free-floating exchange rate was ideal.
On fiscal policy, he favored balanced budgets and lower government spending, and he doubted the PAN would be able to cut taxes, even if it promises to.

Asked how willing the PAN had shown itself to take his advice, Katz was non-committal. He said one of the main problems with the party was that different party chieftains said different things, often contradicting each other, with little internal party discipline.

"The problem is that for almost 70 years their only struggle has been for democracy. What they now need to do is say, 'now we have democracy, imperfect but it's there, and we have to move to the next step, which is discussing the issues.'
"That is what many have not understood," he said.
((-- Mexico City newsroom +525 728-9560))
